title: Google Account Security Checklist: 8 Settings to Check
html:
Open Google's Security Checkup first. It lists what needs fixing on your account and takes a few minutes. Then go through the settings below: a unique password or a passkey, 2-Step Verification, recovery details, the devices signed in to your account, and the apps linked to it. Do this once now, and again once a year.

Last updated: 10 Oct 2026. Google moves menus around from time to time, so the page names below are the ones Google's help pages use today.

I walked through the Security and sign-in page of my own Google Account on 10 Oct 2026.

1. Take the Security Checkup

Go to myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. Google says you should take a Security Checkup regularly. It gives you personal recommendations, such as adding recovery options, creating passkeys, turning on 2-Step Verification and removing risky app access.

My Security and sign-in page showed "You have security tips" and pointed me to the Security Checkup. I only looked at the page and did not change any setting while writing this.

2. Use a unique password, or a passkey

Google says it is not safe to use the same password on multiple sites, and recommends a strong, unique password for each account, kept in a password manager. A passkey is better still: it lets you sign in with your fingerprint, face scan or phone screen lock, and, in Google's words, it cannot be shared, copied, written down or accidentally given to someone else. To create one, go to myaccount.google.com/signinoptions/passkeys and tap Create a passkey. Your phone needs a screen lock turned on first.

3. Turn on 2-Step Verification

Open your Google Account, go to Security and sign-in, and under "How you sign in to Google" choose Turn on 2-Step Verification. Google recommends passkeys as the strongest second step, because they only exist on your devices. It also recommends Google prompts, which you approve with a tap. An authenticator app works without internet or mobile service. Text-message codes are on the list, but they are the weakest option. Keep your backup codes somewhere safe.

For how the methods compare, see our two-factor authentication guide.

4. Check your recovery phone and email

In Security and sign-in, open Recovery phone and Recovery email. Google says recovery information helps you get back into your account if you forget the password or someone else gets in. It suggests an email address you use regularly but not the one you sign in with. A change to the recovery phone can take up to 7 days to take effect. A number you no longer control can end up with someone else, so remove old ones. See what happens to your old phone number.

5. Look at the devices signed in

In your Google Account, go to Security and sign-in, find the Your devices panel and choose Manage all devices. Tap any device or session you do not recognise and choose Sign out. Several sessions can share one device name, so you may need to sign out of more than one.

6. Remove linked apps you no longer use

Go to myaccount.google.com/linkedapps. Google says you can review or remove the apps that have some access to your Google Account data at any time. Those can include "Sign in with Google" connections. Remove what you do not use.

7. Keep the phone and apps updated

Google's list of basics includes keeping your browser, operating system and apps up to date, and uninstalling apps and extensions you do not need. On Android, see our phone maintenance guide for the menus.

8. Do not hand your password to anyone

Google says it never asks for your password in an email, message or phone call. If a message tells you to "verify" your account through a link, open the Google app or type the address yourself instead. If you did enter your password on a page you doubt, change it now, then follow our checks for a compromised phone and Google's steps to secure a compromised account.

What to do next

  1. Take the Security Checkup and fix what it flags.
  2. Turn on 2-Step Verification and create a passkey.
  3. Check recovery details, devices and linked apps.
  4. Repeat once a year, and after any scare.
